title: Gallium chain
eyebrow: Product-chain pilot · the chip metal that became a lever
h1: China makes almost all the gallium — then made it a lever
deck: Gallium is not mined for itself: it is a trace by-product of refining aluminium and zinc, and China produces about 98% of the world's primary supply. In July 2023 it placed gallium under export licensing — the archetype of the export-control playbook this atlas keeps meeting. Gallium goes into the GaN and GaAs chips behind radar, 5G, EV power electronics and LEDs.
byline: bauxite / zinc (the host) ≠ by-product gallium (~98% CN) ≠ high-purity GaAs / GaN ≠ radar, 5G, power chips
correction: Gallium is the cleanest example of the atlas's recurring lever. No one runs a gallium mine — it is extracted in tiny amounts during alumina (Bayer-process) and zinc refining, so it cannot be scaled on its own, and China refines ~98% of it. That concentration became an instrument in July 2023, when China required export licences for gallium and germanium — throttling a material that gates compound-semiconductor chips for defence and communications.

sections.h2: 1 · The by-product trap, at its most extreme

panels.text: Because gallium occurs at parts-per-million in bauxite and zinc ores, supply is welded to alumina and zinc refining — and to whoever chose to install recovery circuits. China did, at scale and low cost, and now produces about 98% of primary gallium. The Western world has the host ores and refineries but largely stopped recovering the gallium because China's was cheaper.

panels.h3: So it cannot be scaled on its own
panels.text: Gallium production is capped by how much alumina and zinc the world refines, not by gallium demand — the same by-product coupling as indium, germanium and rhenium elsewhere in this atlas. You cannot simply 'mine more gallium'; you recover more of what is already flowing through existing refineries, which takes capital and time to retrofit.
panels.flag: coupled to alumina and zinc, not to demand

panels.h3: Export licensing on a defence-critical chip metal
panels.text: In July 2023 China required export licences for gallium and germanium, and Chinese gallium exports fell sharply. Gallium matters because gallium-nitride (GaN) and gallium-arsenide (GaAs) make the high-frequency, high-power chips in military radar and electronic warfare, 5G base stations, satellite communications and increasingly EV power inverters — so the control lands on both defence and the digital build-out (see the defence and silicon-chip chains).
panels.flag: the export-control playbook, in its purest form

sections.h2: 3 · The response: recover what was being discarded

panels.text: Because gallium is technically recoverable from many existing alumina and zinc plants, the fix is industrial rather than geological: restart or add recovery circuits in Europe, North America and elsewhere, plus recycling from GaAs wafer scrap. It is a built chokepoint that can be rebuilt — but qualifying new high-purity supply into defence and semiconductor lines takes years, so the leverage is real in the meantime.

trade_intro: Gallium has no clean HS6 line — unwrought gallium sits in the shared 811292 'other minor metals' basket with indium and germanium, so its trade cannot be isolated (the same limit the atlas flags for indium).
